In [[Filtering problem (stochastic processes)|filtering theory]] the '''Kushner equation''' (after [[Harold J. Kushner|Harold Kushner]]) is an equation for the [[conditional probability]] [[probability density function|density]] of the state of a [[stochastic process|stochastic]] non-linear [[dynamical system]], given noisy measurements of the state.<ref>{{cite journal |authorlink=Harold J. Kushner |last=Kushner |first=H. J. |year=1964 |title=On the differential equations satisfied by conditional probability densities of Markov processes, with applications |journal= Journal of the Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics, Series A: Control|volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=106–119 |doi=10.1137/0302009 }}</ref>  It therefore provides the solution of the [[nonlinear filter]]ing problem in [[estimation theory]]. The equation is sometimes referred to as the '''Stratonovich–Kushner'''<ref>[[Ruslan L. Stratonovich|Stratonovich, R.L.]] (1959). ''Optimum nonlinear systems which bring about a separation of a signal with constant parameters from noise''. Radiofizika, 2:6, pp.&nbsp;892&ndash;901.</ref><ref>[[Ruslan L. Stratonovich|Stratonovich, R.L.]] (1959). ''On the theory of optimal non-linear filtering of random functions''. Theory of Probability and Its Applications, 4, pp.&nbsp;223&ndash;225.</ref><ref>[[Ruslan L. Stratonovich|Stratonovich, R.L.]] (1960) ''Application of the Markov processes theory to optimal filtering''. Radio Engineering and Electronic Physics, 5:11, pp.&nbsp;1&ndash;19.</ref><ref>[[Ruslan L. Stratonovich|Stratonovich, R.L.]] (1960). ''Conditional Markov Processes''. Theory of Probability and Its Applications, 5, pp.&nbsp;156&ndash;178.</ref> (or Kushner–Stratonovich) '''equation'''. {{clarify|text=However, the correct equation in terms of [[Itō calculus]] was first derived by Kushner although a more heuristic Stratonovich version of it appeared already in [[Ruslan Stratonovich|Stratonovich]]'s works in late fifties. However, the derivation in terms of Itō calculus is due to Richard Bucy.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Bucy |first=R. S. |year=1965 |title=Nonlinear filtering theory |journal=IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control |volume=10 |issue=2 |page=198 |doi=10.1109/TAC.1965.1098109 }}</ref>|date=September 2020|reason=It's unclear who derived what and how.}}

== Overview ==

Assume the state of the system evolves according to

:<math>dx = f(x,t) \, dt + \sigma\, dw</math>

and a noisy measurement of the system state is available:

:<math>dz = h(x,t) \, dt + \eta\, dv</math>

where ''w'', ''v'' are independent [[Wiener process]]es. Then the conditional probability density ''p''(''x'',&nbsp;''t'') of the state at time ''t'' is given by the Kushner equation:

:<math>dp(x,t) = L[p(x,t)] dt + p(x,t) \big(h(x,t)-E_t h(x,t) \big)^\top \eta^{-\top}\eta^{-1} \big(dz-E_t h(x,t) dt\big).</math>

where 
:<math>L[p] := -\sum \frac{\partial (f_i p)}{\partial x_i} + \frac{1}{2} \sum (\sigma \sigma^\top)_{i,j} \frac{\partial^2 p}{\partial x_i \partial x_j}</math> 
is the [[Fokker–Planck equation|Kolmogorov forward]] operator and 
:<math>dp(x,t) = p(x,t + dt) - p(x,t)</math> 
is the variation of the conditional probability.

The term <math>dz - E_t h(x,t) dt</math> is the [[innovation (signal processing)|innovation]], i.e. the difference between the measurement and its expected value.

=== Kalman–Bucy filter ===

One can use the Kushner equation to derive the [[Kalman–Bucy filter]] for a linear [[diffusion process]]. Suppose we have <math> f(x,t) = A x</math> and <math> h(x,t) = C x </math>. The Kushner equation will be given by
:<math>
dp(x,t) = L[p(x,t)] dt + p(x,t) \big( C x- C \mu(t) \big)^\top \eta^{-\top}\eta^{-1} \big(dz-C \mu(t) dt\big),
</math>
where <math> \mu(t) </math> is the mean of the conditional probability at time <math> t</math>. Multiplying by <math> x</math> and integrating over it, we obtain the variation of the mean
:<math>
d\mu(t) = A \mu(t) dt + \Sigma(t) C^\top \eta^{-\top}\eta^{-1} \big(dz - C\mu(t) dt\big).
</math>
Likewise, the variation of the variance <math>\Sigma(t)</math> is given by
:<math>
\tfrac{d}{dt}\Sigma(t) = A\Sigma(t) + \Sigma(t) A^\top + \sigma^\top \sigma-\Sigma(t) C^\top\eta^{-\top} \eta^{-1} C \,\Sigma(t).
</math>
The conditional probability is then given at every instant by a normal distribution <math>\mathcal{N}(\mu(t),\Sigma(t))</math>.
